title: The prophets answer
hookLine: a reading from the prophets follows the Torah on Shabbat and festivals

lines: A MELODY THROUGH A BEDROOM DOOR.
cards: For months, a melody has leaked through a bedroom door: a teenager practicing, stopping, starting the same line again. Then the Saturday comes.

The family fills the front rows, the voice cracks once on a high note, and the whole room holds its breath until the last word. Ask what that teenager was chanting, and the answer is often: my haftarah.
Ask what a haftarah is, and why it comes after the Torah, and the room may go quiet. It isn't from the Torah scroll at all.

teach.b: On Shabbat, festivals and fast days, after the Torah reading, one more person is called up, the maftir.
They read the last few verses of the portion again, then a passage from the Prophets, from books like Isaiah, Jeremiah, Samuel or Kings.
That passage is the haftarah. The word comes from a root meaning to conclude, to complete. It isn't half of anything; it's the closing reading.
Each haftarah is chosen to answer the Torah portion. When the Torah tells of Moses sending spies into the land, the haftarah tells of Joshua sending spies to Jericho.
Around the summer fast of Tisha b'Av, the pattern takes over the calendar: three haftarot of warning before the fast, then seven of comfort after it. The first of the seven opens Isaiah forty.
In the old Jewish translation: "Comfort ye, comfort ye My people, saith your God." Why read the Prophets at all?
A popular explanation, written down in the Middle Ages, says that when a foreign king banned Torah reading, Jews read matching passages from the Prophets instead.
Historians aren't sure that's how it began; the Mishnah already lays down rules for the reading. Either way, the shape says something.
The Torah speaks, and the prophets answer: later voices taking up the same story, centuries on, asking what it means now.

how: On Shabbat, festivals and fast days the maftir reads the closing verses of the Torah portion and then chants the haftarah from the Prophets, with blessings before and after; many bar and bat mitzvah students chant it as their portion.

games.q: this week's Torah portion tells of Moses sending spies into the land. you're choosing a reading from the Prophets to answer it. which fits?
games.why: the haftarah for that portion is Joshua's spies at Jericho: the prophets answer the Torah with a matching story.

practice: If you have a Bible nearby, open to Isaiah, Jeremiah, Amos or Micah, anywhere, and read one line slowly; if not, take today's line: comfort ye, comfort ye My people.
Ask who needed to hear it the day it was first said, and let one face come to mind who might need it now.
